title: Cheap eats, work in Scranton and Omaha, and Mamie Lee Kelly
summary: Life in New Orleans with Stale Bread and Kid Ross, a stage manager's offer, a piano job in Scranton, and later work in Omaha where he played for Mamie Lee Kelly.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Yeah. Yeah, I know that. A dollar and a half, a dollar and a half a week. Yeah. He introduced me to red beans and rice at the Chinamans for a nickel. I swear. China's eating in the world. And they sold, they sold two, two pork chops for a dime. Well, they used to go in Martins, in the alley, and have a big piece of roast beef there. They'd give you one slice of bread cutting and put that roast beef on it. And they had free lunch, free lunch, a bunch of cheese and stuff and stuff. And there comes along a fellow with a big hamper, biggest hamper ever seen, full of shrimp. Ten for a nickel. Ten for a nickel. I mean big ones. Yeah. Nickel. That's true. Well, I stayed around, oh yes, I wasn't there long when my father's friend, Mr. Gibson, who was the stage manager for Talk on the York Show, one of the George N. Cohen Show. I was living at the Bush Hotel with another piano player named Kid Ross for seven dollars a week. Later he was called a senator. There were nice rooms. The fellow says, hey, bars, this is Mr. Gibson, so why don't you go home? So I went home, I told my father I wanted to go for my soap. So I finally went out with a sign painter out of New York City, painting all that I do is the fellow around that was black, see. They had a regular painter with him, see. There was three in one oil, two of the advertisements, I forget the other ones, see. And we got to Scranton, Pennsylvania. He liked to sing this, my boss that I worked for, see. He had a loud, loud voice, like, hey, the foot of stars are shining, all that kind of stuff. So the fellow was sitting at the piano, happened to be the owner of this Conway Hotel, they call it the Conway House, that's just called the smaller places around Scranton. And he says, you want a job? I said, I don't play for a living. I'll give you fifteen dollars a week and borrow the larger. The coal miners were making fifteen dollars a week, that's all they were making. I mean, hard coal, anthracite coal. So I got, so I'm going back to New Orleans, I couldn't say where. I made three trips back in fourth New Orleans. And the last trip, I was in Omaha playing for Gus Wick, whose wife was a lady in blue at the, at the, at the, uh. Blue Rose? Yeah. See. Well, I stayed at his house about three weeks, they opened the place, you know. And, uh, that's where I met Mamie Lee Kelly. Mamie Lee Kelly, I went and worked for her two nights, she never paid me.
When Gus Wick opened up, we had a makeup box.
Ben Bard, who married Ruth Holland, and, uh, Martha Pryor, beautiful boxing girl, saying, I ain't got no body, don't shake my tree. Pieces, something like that.
